prime.problem: Without a method, kernel tuning is guesswork: you try tricks at random and can't tell whether a 2× win is possible or whether you are already at the hardware's floor. The course's 16 cards are a pile of tricks until you can say which bound each one attacks.
prime.fits: This is the course map. It builds on perf-1's roofline (a kernel is limited by math or by bytes) and adds the third cost that roofline hides: idle time from launches, stalls and unhidden latency. Every later card is one move inside this loop.
expect: the four levers: fewer bytes, faster math, hide latency, cut overhead
prime.goal: Look at any kernel's numbers, name which bound it sits at, pick the family of fixes that can move it, and predict roughly how much there is left to gain.

attend: In T ≥ max(F/C, Q/W) + T_idle, which term is fixed by the problem and which ones does the kernel's design choose?
siboehm's 4092² matmul has a 4.57 ms math floor and a 0.35 ms byte floor, yet the naive kernel takes 0.444 s. Which term of the formula is it losing to?
Why does the overview put occupancy, ILP and more work per thread in their own bucket, separate from both memory-bound and compute-bound fixes?
The lever table's rows don't multiply to the ladder's 75×. What does that say about applying levers one after another?
When would an inference engineer at a serving company never write any of these kernels, and what would they still need from this course?

must: A kernel's time ≥ max(math floor F/C, byte floor Q_moved/W) + idle time → F is fixed by the problem, but Q_moved and T_idle are set by the kernel's design → almost every optimization shrinks Q_moved or T_idle, not F

Intensity F/Q_moved vs the ridge C/W → below the ridge, fewer bytes is the only lever (coalesce, tile, fuse, lower precision) → above it, only faster math units help (tensor cores, FP8) → so you must place the kernel before choosing a fix

Neither DRAM nor math saturated → the GPU is waiting on latency or issuing overhead instructions → the fix is more independent work in flight (warps, ILP, more outputs per thread) or less bookkeeping (unrolling, cascading), not fewer bytes
Many small kernels → launch gaps rival each kernel's own time (~2 µs per launch vs a 3.8 µs vector add on an H100) → fusion and CUDA graphs remove launches → this bound matters most at batch-1 decode
Structural steps (launch enough threads, coalesce, tile, reuse from registers) close most of the gap → the last 20% costs twice the effort and doesn't transfer between GPUs → the power law of effort
elevated: Nsight Compute stall reasons separate latency (long_scoreboard) from bandwidth (memory throughput near peak) → the same low GB/s can mean opposite fixes, which is why you profile before choosing
reference: the lever table's individual speed-ups and which GPU each was measured on
Hopper vocabulary: TMA, thread-block clusters (8 portable, 16 opt-in), warp specialization, tcgen05
the source quirks (268 vs 278 MB, 30 vs 38.7 TF, the A100 slip, T4 at 300 vs 320 GB/s)

compress.prompt: Draw the whole course's causal map from memory: the time formula in the middle, the four bounds around it (memory, compute, latency/instruction, overhead), and for each bound the cards whose tricks attack it. Then add one arrow for the loop: measure → place → fix → re-measure.
checklist: time floor = max(math, bytes actually moved) + idle, and only the math term is fixed by the problem
placing the kernel (intensity vs ridge, plus stall reasons) decides which family of fixes can help
memory-bound: coalescing, shared-memory tiling, fusion, lower precision
compute-bound: tensor cores and lower-precision math
latency/instruction-bound: occupancy, ILP, more outputs per thread, unrolling and cascading
overhead-bound: fusion and CUDA graphs; tuning after the structural steps gives diminishing, GPU-specific returns

retrieve.q: Explain why the same 4092² matmul can be described as compute-bound and yet a kernel for it can run at 1% of peak, using the two floors and the bytes the kernel actually moves.
answer: the problem's floors: 4.57 ms of math vs 0.35 ms of minimum bytes on the A6000, so a good kernel is compute-bound
the naive kernel's design moves up to 548 GB (2,046× the minimum), so its own byte term dwarfs the math
compute-bound describes the problem; the kernel's Q_moved decides where the kernel actually sits

retrieve.q: Walk through the loop on a kernel you've never seen: what do you run first, what do you read off it, and how does that choose between coalescing, tensor cores, more warps and CUDA graphs?
answer: nsys timeline: where the time goes, which kernel is on top, whether there are launch gaps
ncu on the top kernel: % of peak FLOP/s and GB/s, intensity vs ridge, stall reasons
high GB/s, low FLOP/s → fewer bytes; high FLOP/s → faster math; neither → latency/instruction fixes; gaps → graphs or fusion
re-measure after each fix, because the bound moves

retrieve.q: siboehm's first four steps give 51.7× in two weekends and the last four give 1.46× in four more. At a kernel company, when is chasing the last 1.46× worth it, and what do you give up?
answer: worth it for kernels that dominate fleet time (the main GEMMs, attention) where 5–10% is real money
the tuned configs don't transfer: the A6000's best is 0.95× of the best on an A100
you give up time and portability; for most kernels, pick a library kernel and fuse around it

retrieve.q: Which bound does each of these live at, and which card's fix applies: a batch-1 decode step of 323 small kernels, the naive transpose, siboehm's kernel 3, and a BF16 prefill GEMM on an H100?
answer: decode step: overhead (launch gaps a real share of the 4.79 ms floor) → fusion and CUDA graphs
naive transpose: memory, 12.5% sector efficiency on writes → stage through shared memory
kernel 3: shared-memory instruction throughput (MIO throttle) → more results per thread
BF16 prefill GEMM: compute → tensor cores, then FP8

compare.q: perf-1's roofline has two floors; this course's formula adds T_idle and separates minimum bytes from bytes moved. What does each addition let you explain that the plain roofline can't, and how would the plain roofline mislead you on a naive kernel?
answer: bytes moved vs minimum explains why a compute-bound problem can have a memory-bound kernel (548 GB vs 268 MB)
T_idle explains decode steps where neither roof is reached because the GPU waits on launches
the plain roofline would place the naive matmul at intensity 512 and predict compute-bound speed it never gets

compare.q: perf-2 models a whole decode step's time from weights and KV bytes; this course models one kernel. Where do the two models meet, and what does kernel-level work change in perf-2's step-time estimate?
answer: both are max(math, bytes) floors, at different granularity
perf-2 assumes kernels run near their roofs; this course is about closing the gap to those roofs
kernel work changes the achieved fraction of the floor (and launch overhead), not the floor itself; lower precision changes the floor

predict.q: A Llama-3.1-8B decode step at batch 1 on an H100 has a 4.79 ms byte floor. You swap every GEMM for a kernel that runs twice as fast at the same bytes. Commit: roughly how much faster does the step get, and why?
predict.answer: Almost not at all. At batch 1 every GEMM is a matrix-vector product with intensity about 1 FLOP/B, so its time is set by reading the weights, not by math. A kernel that is "2× faster" in compute moves the same 16.06 GB, so the floor stays 4.79 ms. What can move the step is fewer bytes (FP8 weights: 209 → 417 tok/s ceiling) or less idle time (graphs and fusion shaving the launch gaps).

apply.task: Place five kernels on the two ridges without looking anything up, then check. Ridges: T4 FP32 ≈ 25 FLOP/B, H100 BF16 ≈ 295. Kernels: (1) FP32 vector add (1 add per 12 bytes), (2) the reduction sum (1 add per 4 bytes), (3) the naive matmul counted with no cache (0.25 FLOP/B), (4) a well-tiled 4092² FP32 matmul at its minimum traffic, (5) the batch-1 Llama up-projection GEMV (1.0 FLOP/B). For each, name the bound on each GPU and the one card whose fix you'd reach for first.
apply.done: You have a 5-row table with intensity, bound on T4, bound on H100 and the card to open, and only kernel 4 is on the compute side of either ridge.
apply.hint: Intensities: 1/12 ≈ 0.083, 0.25, 0.25, 137.1 GFLOP ÷ 267.9 MB ≈ 512, and 1.0. Only 512 clears 25 and 295. Kernel 3's fix is reuse (matmul II/III), kernels 1, 2 and 5 are memory-bound whatever you do, so the fix is fewer bytes or batching (for 5).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the decode step, or one of the five placements?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why bytes moved differs from minimum bytes, or why latency-bound is its own bucket?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: intensity → bound, or bound → which card's fix?
Which of the four levers have you actually seen measured on a card, and which only as a claim?
What will you revisit before the matmul cards: the lower-bound arithmetic, or the stall reasons?
